questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(0,1)$ to the point $N(3,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx-y\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t(3\,i+3\,j-j) \\  & =j+t(3\,i+2\,j) \\  & =3t\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=3t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=3\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx-y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3t)^{2}\cdot 3-(1+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}27{t}^{2}-2-4t\,dt \\  & ={[9{t}^{3}-2t-2{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[9(1)^{3}-2(1)-2(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(-1,1)$ to the point $N(1,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+{x}^{2}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+j$ and $b=i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =-i+j+t(i+3\,j-(-i+j)) \\  & =-i+j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t-1$ and $y(t)=2t+1$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+{x}^{2}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+1)^{2}\cdot 2+(2t-1)^{2}\cdot 2\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+4t+1)+(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}8{t}^{2}+2\,dt \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}+1\,dt \\  & =4{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4[\frac{4}{3}+10]-4[0] \\  & =\frac{28}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(1,2)$ to the point $B(3,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+2\,j$ and $b=3\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+2\,j+t(3\,i+4\,j-(i+2\,j)) \\  & =i+2\,j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(1+2t)\,i+(2+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=1+2t$ and $y(t)=2+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+2t)\cdot 2+(2+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6+8t\,dt \\  & ={[6t+4{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[6(1)+4(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(-1,2)$ to the point $B(1,0),$ then ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+2\,j$ and $b=i.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =-i+2\,j+t(i-(-i+2\,j)) \\  & =-i+2\,j+t(2\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t-1$ and $y(t)=2-2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-1)(2-2t)(2)+(-2)\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-1)(2-2t)-1\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}-4{t}^{2}+6t-3\,dt \\  & =2{[-\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+3{t}^{2}-3t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2[-\frac{4}{3}+3-3]-2[0] \\  & =2[-\frac{4}{3}] \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(4,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,dx-{e}^{x+y}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0\,i+0\,j$ and $b=4\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0\,i+0\,j+t(4\,i+2\,j-(0\,i+0\,j)) \\  & =4t\,i+2t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=4t$ and $y(t)=2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=4\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,dx-{e}^{x+y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x+y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-{e}^{x+y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x+y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{4t+2t}(4-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6t}}{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6(1)}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{6(0)}}{3} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6}}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6}-1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=\pi {x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(1,\pi )$ to point $B(2,4\pi ),$ then ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\pi {x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+\pi {t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2\pi t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi {t}^{2}}{2{t}^{2}})\cdot 1+3t\cdot 2\pi t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}1+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & =[t+2\pi {t}^{3}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =[2+2\pi (2)^{3}]-[1+2\pi (1)^{3}] \\  & =[2+16\pi ]-[1+2\pi ] \\  & =1+14\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{3}$ traversed from the point $P(1,1)$ to point $Q(2,8),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+3\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+3t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})}+3(2)]-[-\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}+3(1)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}+6+\frac{1}{2}-3 \\  & =\frac{27}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=\sqrt{x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then  ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({({t}^{2})}^{2}+t)\cdot 2t+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+t)\cdot 2t+3{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{5}+5{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{(1)^{6}}{3}+\frac{5(1)^{3}}{3}+(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{3}+1]-[0] \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ traversed from the point $P(0,0)$ to point $Q(1,1),$ then ${\int }_{C}4y{e}^{xy}\,dx+dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt[3]{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{3}\,i+t\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4y{e}^{xy}\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4y{e}^{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4y{e}^{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t\cdot {e}^{{t}^{3}\cdot t}\cdot 3{t}^{2}+1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{4}}+1\,dt \\  & ={[3{e}^{{t}^{4}}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[3{e}^{(1)^{4}}+(1)]-[3{e}^{(0)^{4}}+(0)] \\  & =[3e+1]-[3] \\  & =3e-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=\pi {x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,\pi ),$ then ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})\,dx+4{x}^{2}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\pi {x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+\pi {t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2\pi t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})\,dx+4{x}^{2}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+4{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+4{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi {t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}})\cdot 1+4{t}^{2}\cdot 2\pi t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +8\pi {t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8\pi {t}^{3}-1\,dt \\  & =[2\pi {t}^{4}-t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =[2\pi (1)^{4}-1]-[0] \\  & =2\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dy-x\,dx}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dy-x\,dx}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {y}^{′}\,\text{d}t-x\cdot {x}^{′}\,\text{d}t}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {y}^{′}-x\cdot {x}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[-1-1] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(0,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}((x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}6-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\frac{2}{y}\,dx+y{e}^{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{2}{y}\,dx+y{e}^{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2}{y}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y{e}^{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{2}{y}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+y{e}^{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-1\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,\sqrt{3})$ to the point $B(-\sqrt{3},0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+3\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx-{x}^{2}\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx-{x}^{2}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-{sin}^{3}⁡t-{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t+{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
canonical_examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overline{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1, 1),$ calculate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^2y\,\mathrm{d}x + xy\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a} = 0\,\mathbf{i} + 0\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = 1\,\mathbf{i} + 1\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ So, we have that $x(t) = t$ and $y(t) = t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot t\cdot 1+t\cdot t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=x^2$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ evaluate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + (x-y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y = x^2.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+1-\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14059731/assets/7a6e67435aab40d5bf3630c66f79241008357e1549b1c77b4c0bdfea2b453883.png)

Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \dfrac{y\,\mathrm{d}x - x\,\mathrm{d}y}{x^2+y^2},$ where $C$ is a part of the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $\left(0,2\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that a parametrization for the given path is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dx-x\,dy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {x}^{′}-x\cdot {y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}},dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,dt \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
